engagement.coverage_declaration: Families exercised: WSTG-ATHZ-* and ASVS 5.0 V8 (route-by-route authorization of the HTTP surface, including the /api/* handler set and the basic-auth middleware); WSTG-INPV-* and ASVS 5.0 V1/V5 (comment-to-argv flow into terraform, git ref and path validators, repo/var-file allowlists); ASVS 5.0 V11 (request-body and allocation bounds on unauthenticated endpoints); WSTG-CLNT-* (WebSocket handshake origin handling); WSTG-ERRH-* and ASVS 5.0 V16 (error and log content on the webhook and API paths); CICD-SEC-* (GitHub Actions triggers, permissions and action pinning); plus a repository-wide distinctive-format secret scan. Families NOT exercised: no dependency-advisory or reachability analysis was performed against go.sum or package-lock.json, so A03:2025 and SLSA supply-chain claims are absent, not clean; the six VCS provider clients under server/events/vcs/** were not read, so approval, mergeability and team-membership logic per provider is unaudited; the persistence layer (boltdb, redis, planstore, locking) was not read, so lock-key handling, plan-artifact storage and the S3 plan store are unaudited; the web UI HTML templates were not read (only the fact that server/controllers/web_templates/web_templates.go uses html/template rather than text/template), so WSTG-CLNT-* XSS coverage of the UI is partial; the job output/logging path and the outbound notification webhooks were not read. findings.title: GET /api/locks answers without authentication while every sibling /api/* handler requires the API token, and /api/ is exempt from web basic auth
findings.evidence: ListLocks (api_controller.go:383-410) obtains the middleware only to reuse its Responder and then calls a.Locker.List() directly; it never calls middleware.RequireAuth(w, r) and never inspects a.APISecret. Every other handler on the same controller does: DriftStatus (line 421), Remediate (line 1129), GetRemediationResult (line 1729), ListRemediationResults (line 1841) and DetectDrift (line 2082) all open with `if !middleware.RequireAuth(w, r) { return }`, and Plan (282) / Apply (315) authenticate inside apiParseAndValidate (line 1009-1017, subtle.ConstantTimeCompare against a.APISecret). The route is registered unconditionally at server/server.go:1212. The only other gate is the negroni middleware in server/middleware.go, whose allow-list at lines 37-43 ends with `strings.HasPrefix(r.URL.Path, "/api/")`, so basic auth is skipped for this path. The response body carries, per lock: repository full name, project name, project path, pull request number and URL, the username that holds the lock, workspace and timestamp. The same data set is rendered by the web index at server/server.go:1350-1373, which is NOT exempt and is therefore gated by basic auth.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated client that can reach the Atlantis HTTP port retrieves an inventory of the repositories, project paths, open pull request numbers and URLs, and the usernames of the engineers holding locks - the same data an operator deliberately placed behind --web-basic-auth on the index page. For a self-hosted Atlantis serving private repositories this is internal reconnaissance material (repository names, active change surface, valid usernames) obtained with no credential.
findings.preconditions: Network reach to the Atlantis listener. The finding is about the gap between the two paths, so it matters when the operator has enabled --web-basic-auth (and/or set --api-secret) expecting the surface to be gated; with both disabled the whole web UI is open anyway and /api/locks adds nothing.
findings.recommendation: Call `middleware.RequireAuth(w, r)` at the top of ListLocks exactly as the sibling handlers do, so the endpoint fails closed when --api-secret is unset. Independently, stop exempting the whole `/api/` prefix in server/middleware.go:43 and exempt only the specific paths that carry their own token check, so a future handler added without RequireAuth is not silently unauthenticated as well. If the endpoint is genuinely meant to be public, say so in code rather than by omission and strip the usernames and pull request URLs from the payload.

triage.reason: The only layer in front of the router is RequestLogger.ServeHTTP (server/middleware.go:34-63); its allow-list at line 43 explicitly matches the /api/ prefix, so it is not a control that covers this route - it is the reason the route is uncovered.

No artifact in the target claims an external gate. The repository ships its own two access controls (--web-basic-auth in server/middleware.go and --api-secret in server/controllers/api_response.go:213-228) and runatlantis.io/docs/security.md presents them as the mechanism; nothing in Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, kustomize/ or the docs places a mandatory authenticating proxy in front.

Read directly: ListLocks is an ordinary registered mux handler (server/server.go:1212) whose body contains no authorization call. There is no base type, decorator or interface indirection in this controller - the sibling handlers make the check inline in their own bodies.

runatlantis.io/docs/api-endpoints.md:951 does state that most endpoints in that section need no token, so the exposure is intended in isolation. It is not bounded, though: the identical data is gated on the index page (server/server.go:1350), so an operator who enables --web-basic-auth is told the lock listing is protected while /api/locks still serves it. An intended exposure that defeats a control the same product offers is not FP-05 - and per that rule the finding moves rather than disappears, to the middleware exemption.

findings.limits: This establishes only that the endpoint is readable without credentials and what it returns. It does not establish that the lock data is sensitive in any particular deployment, and it establishes nothing about the write-side lock routes (DELETE /locks, POST /apply/lock), which are not in the /api/ exemption and are therefore covered by basic auth when it is enabled.

findings.title: The --var-file-allowlist check matches only the single-dash spelling, so `--var-file=<path>` in a pull request comment reaches terraform unchecked
findings.evidence: Check (var_file_allowlist_checker.go:37-56) recognises a var-file argument in exactly two shapes: the two-token form guarded by `flag == "-var-file"` (line 40) and the joined form guarded by `len(flagSplit) == 2 && flagSplit[0] == "-var-file"` (line 46). Both comparisons are string equality against the single-dash spelling. Anything else falls through with path == "" and is not tested by isAllowedPath at all. The arguments being tested are the raw extra args a commenter typed after `--`: comment_parser.go:378-390 collects them from pflag's ArgsLenAtDash() into CommentCommand.Flags, and the only filter applied on the way is isBlockedExtraArg (comment_parser.go:399-406) against DefaultBlockedExtraArgs, which is `-chdir, --chdir, -plugin-dir, --plugin-dir` (comment_parser.go:50-55) and contains no var-file entry. Those same Flags become ProjectContext.CommentArgs and are appended verbatim to the terraform argv in plan_step_runner.go:153 (buildPlanCmd) and executed through NewArgvCommandRunner. That the two spellings are interchangeable for the Terraform CLI is asserted by this repository itself: DefaultBlockedExtraArgs blocks both `-chdir` and `--chdir`, and both `-plugin-dir` and `--plugin-dir`, under a comment describing them as 'Terraform CLI flag prefixes'. The same single-dash-only shape recurs in ApplyStepRunner.hasTargetFlag (server/core/runtime/apply_step_runner.go:92-97), which rejects `-target` on apply but not `--target`.
findings.impact: The control that runatlantis.io/docs/security.md:64-69 describes as the mitigation for 'the files on your Atlantis install may be accessible as variable definition files from pull requests' is bypassed by changing one character. Anyone able to comment on a pull request in an allow-listed repository can make the Atlantis process read a file of their choosing outside the allow-list (default: the data directory only) as a Terraform variable definitions file - cloud credential files, ~/.terraformrc with registry tokens, a mounted service-account token, /proc/self/environ. Terraform surfaces the file back to the commenter either as loaded variable values or, for a file that is not valid HCL, as a parse diagnostic that quotes the offending source; Atlantis posts terraform output to the pull request and streams it to the job log.
findings.preconditions: The repository is in --repo-allowlist, the attacker can comment on one of its pull requests, and `plan` is in --allow-commands (it is, by default). If --gh-team-allowlist-command or the team allowlist is configured the attacker must also pass it. No non-default server flag is required.
findings.recommendation: Normalise the argument before matching instead of comparing against one literal: strip a leading run of dashes, split on the first '=' only, and then compare the flag name - the same normalisation applies to isBlockedExtraArg and to hasTargetFlag. Prefer an allow-list of permitted extra-arg flag names over a deny-list. Also fix the `len(flagSplit) == 2` condition at line 46: a value containing '=' (`-var-file=/a/b=c`) produces three parts today and skips the check entirely. Add table-driven tests covering `--var-file`, `--var-file=`, `-var-file=` with an '=' in the value, and `--target`.
findings.inference: That the Terraform (and OpenTofu) CLI accepts `--var-file` as an equivalent spelling of `-var-file`. I did not execute terraform, and the target tree contains no terraform binary; the inference rests on the repository's own DefaultBlockedExtraArgs listing both spellings of -chdir and -plugin-dir as flags that must be blocked, which is the maintainers' own statement that the double-dash form reaches the CLI.
findings.what_would_settle_it: Run `terraform plan --var-file=/etc/hostname` (and `--target=x`) against any Terraform 1.x binary and observe whether the flag is honoured; equivalently, a unit test that feeds `[]string{"--var-file", "/etc/hostname"}` to VarFileAllowlistChecker.Check and asserts an error, run against a terraform invocation that shows the file was opened.

triage.reason: The only other layer on this path is isBlockedExtraArg (server/events/comment_parser.go:399-406) against DefaultBlockedExtraArgs (lines 50-55), which lists chdir and plugin-dir only. No later stage inspects the argv: plan_step_runner.go:153 flattens CommentArgs into the command unchanged.

The value is the literal text of a pull request comment. events_controller.go:673 passes comment.GetBody() into CommentParser.Parse, and comment_parser.go:378-390 carries the post-`--` tokens through to CommentCommand.Flags without rewriting them.

Whether the terraform binary treats `--var-file` as the var-file flag was not observed - no terraform binary is in the target and no test in the tree exercises the double-dash spelling. This is the single inferred link and the reason the status is `probable` rather than `confirmed`.

The path is in the shipped server: the route (/events), the parser and the checker are all wired in the default configuration; --var-file-allowlist defaults to --data-dir at cmd/server.go:1307-1310 rather than being disabled.

findings.limits: Establishes the gap in the checker and the unmodified path from comment text to terraform argv. It does not establish what Terraform prints for any specific file, and therefore does not establish how much of a given file's content returns to the commenter versus only its existence and a parse error.

findings.title: The var-file allow-list is applied only to the `plan` command, so `atlantis import -- -var-file=<path>` skips it entirely
findings.evidence: checkVarFilesInPlanCommandAllowlisted (command_runner.go:411-417) returns nil immediately unless `cmd.CommandName() == command.Plan`, and it is the only caller of VarFileAllowlistChecker.Check (invoked at command_runner.go:446 from validateCommentCommand). The comment extra args of the other commands reach terraform by the same route: import_step_runner.go:48-50 appends ctx.CommentArgs to `terraform import`, and state_rm_step_runner.go:50 appends them to `terraform state rm`. So for `atlantis import -- -var-file=/path ADDRESS ID` the allow-list is never consulted, with the ordinary single-dash spelling and no reliance on F-002.
findings.impact: Same host-file read as F-002 but reached through a command the allow-list does not cover at all, so an operator who tightened --var-file-allowlist still has an open path. The reader is the Atlantis process, and the output returns to the pull request.
findings.preconditions: `import` (or `state`) must be present in --allow-commands. The default at cmd/server.go:176 is `version,plan,apply,unlock,approve_policies,cancel`, which excludes both, so this requires an operator who has widened --allow-commands - a documented and commonly used configuration, but not the default.
findings.recommendation: Move the var-file check out of the plan-only branch and apply it to every command whose CommentArgs are forwarded to terraform (plan, import, state, and apply on the remote-ops path at apply_step_runner.go:67). Better: apply the extra-arg validation once, where CommentCommand.Flags is built, rather than per command name, so a command added later inherits it.
findings.inference: That `terraform import` accepts -var-file. I did not execute terraform; the tree contains no evidence either way beyond the fact that Atlantis forwards arbitrary comment args to that subcommand.
findings.what_would_settle_it: `terraform import -var-file=/etc/hostname <addr> <id>` against any Terraform 1.x binary - whether the flag is accepted and the file opened before the address is resolved.

triage.reason: No other layer validates extra args for import or state: comment_parser.go:399-406 blocks only chdir and plugin-dir, and import_step_runner.go:48-50 appends CommentArgs without inspection.
The tokens come from the pull request comment body, unchanged from CommentParser.Parse to ProjectContext.CommentArgs.
Terraform's acceptance of -var-file on the `import` subcommand was not observed inside this scope.

The import and state runners are compiled into the shipped binary and registered in the runner map; only the --allow-commands value gates whether a comment can reach them, and that is server configuration, not a build-time exclusion.

findings.limits: Does not establish that any particular deployment enables `import`. Does not cover whether `terraform state rm` accepts -var-file - only that Atlantis would not check it if it did.

findings.title: Webhook and API request bodies are read into memory with io.ReadAll and no size bound anywhere in the server
findings.evidence: `grep -rn "MaxBytesReader|MaxHeaderBytes|LimitReader" server cmd --include=*.go` returns nothing. The http.Server built at server/server.go:1272 sets ReadHeaderTimeout but no MaxHeaderBytes and wraps no body limiter. Every entry point buffers the whole body before it can decide anything: events_controller.go:222 (Bitbucket Cloud) and :252 (Bitbucket Server) read the body BEFORE common.ValidateSignature is called on it; events_controller.go:323 does the same for Gitea; github_request_validator.go:54 and gitlab_request_parser_validator.go:62 read it inside the validators; api_controller.go:1021, :1145 and :2098 read it on the API paths. /events is by design unauthenticated at the transport layer - it is the endpoint the VCS posts to - so the allocation happens for any anonymous POST, and the signature that would reject a forged request is only checked afterwards.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated client that can reach the listener forces the process to allocate memory proportional to the body it sends, with no ceiling and no credential; concurrent requests multiply it. On a container with a memory limit this is an OOM kill of the Atlantis server, which stops plan and apply for every repository it serves.
findings.preconditions: Network reach to the Atlantis listener. No webhook secret is needed, because the read precedes signature verification on the Bitbucket, Gitea, GitHub and GitLab paths.
findings.recommendation: Wrap r.Body in http.MaxBytesReader with a configurable ceiling in a single place - the negroni middleware in server/middleware.go is the natural spot, so every current and future handler inherits it - and set http.Server.MaxHeaderBytes. Size the default above the largest realistic webhook payload (GitHub delivers up to 25 MB) and return 413 above it.
findings.inference: That no fronting layer caps the body in the operator's deployment. Nothing in Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml or kustomize/ places a proxy in front, but a self-hosted product is commonly deployed behind an ingress that sets a body limit, and per FP-08 I must not assume its absence any more than its presence.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The ingress or reverse-proxy configuration for the target install - an nginx `client_max_body_size`, an ALB/Envoy limit, a Kubernetes ingress annotation. Absent such an artifact the Go server itself accepts an unbounded body.

triage.reason: There is no in-repository layer that bounds the body: the grep for MaxBytesReader/LimitReader over server/ and cmd/ is empty, and the single middleware (server/middleware.go:34-63) only logs and applies basic auth.

Whether the operator fronts Atlantis with a proxy that caps request bodies cannot be established from this tree; per FP-08 the answer is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS, and that is why the status is `probable`.
The second principal is any anonymous network client: /events is registered without authentication at server/server.go:1209 and exempted from basic auth at server/middleware.go:38.

findings.limits: Establishes the absence of a bound in the shipped server, not the memory ceiling of any particular deployment, and does not quantify how large a body is needed to kill a given instance.

findings.title: The job-log WebSocket accepts any Origin by default, and websocket.NewWriter hardcodes an always-true origin check that would override the flag for any caller
findings.evidence: checkOriginFunc (websocket/mux.go:36-42) returns nil when checkOrigin is true - letting gorilla apply checkSameOrigin - and an always-true function otherwise. NewMultiplexor wires it correctly from userConfig.WebsocketCheckOrigin (server/server.go:1062-1066), whose default is false (cmd/server.go:688-691), so the live GET /jobs/{job-id}/ws handshake accepts any Origin unless the operator opts in. Separately, NewWriter (writer.go:14-22) builds the upgrader from checkOriginFunc and then, on line 18, unconditionally reassigns `upgrader.CheckOrigin = func(r *http.Request) bool { return true }`, discarding its own parameter. Grep over server/ and cmd/ shows NewWriter has no caller today - the multiplexor constructs its Writer struct literally - so the override is latent rather than live.
findings.impact: With the default configuration a page on any origin the victim visits can open the job-log socket and read streamed terraform output for a job whose id it can name, subject to the multiplexor's IsKeyExists check (websocket/mux.go:67-70). The NewWriter override adds no impact today but guarantees that the first caller of that constructor silently loses the --websocket-check-origin setting.
findings.preconditions: The attacker must know or guess a live job id (a UUID) and the victim's browser must reach the Atlantis host.
findings.recommendation: Delete line 18 of writer.go, or delete NewWriter entirely since nothing calls it - a constructor that ignores its own security parameter is a trap for the next caller. Consider defaulting --websocket-check-origin to true; the flag exists precisely because the permissive behaviour is the wrong default for an internal tool.

triage.reason: The always-true override is in NewWriter, which has no caller: the only construction of a Writer in shipping code is the struct literal inside NewMultiplexor (server/controllers/websocket/mux.go:48-52), which uses checkOriginFunc(checkOrigin) correctly. The override therefore does not exist on any live path.

The permissive default is declared and operator-selectable: cmd/server.go:688-691 sets it and runatlantis.io/docs/server-configuration.md:1737-1745 documents the flag. Per FP-10 the finding stays written down at informational rather than disappearing.

Nothing else authenticates the handshake: Multiplexor.Handle (websocket/mux.go:61-84) checks only that the partition key exists, and /jobs/{job-id}/ws is covered by basic auth only when --web-basic-auth is enabled (server/middleware.go:37-43).

findings.limits: No exploit path is claimed. Whether a browser attaches cached basic-auth credentials to a cross-origin WebSocket handshake against a given Atlantis deployment was not tested, and job-id guessability was not measured.

findings.title: Web basic auth compares username and password with Go string equality rather than a constant-time comparison
findings.evidence: `if user == l.WebUsername && pass == l.WebPassword` (server/middleware.go:49). Go's string == short-circuits on the first differing byte. The same codebase uses the constant-time primitive everywhere else a secret is compared: subtle.ConstantTimeCompare in api_response.go:222 (X-Atlantis-Token), api_controller.go:1016 (the same token on the legacy path) and gitlab_request_parser_validator.go:56 (the GitLab webhook token), and hmac.Equal in vcs/common/request_validation.go:42.
findings.impact: A timing oracle on the web UI password in principle. Over HTTP, against short strings, the signal is far below network jitter, so the practical gain to an attacker is nil - it is recorded because it is the one secret comparison in the tree that does not follow the codebase's own convention.
findings.recommendation: Use subtle.ConstantTimeCompare on both fields, comparing fixed-length digests so the length of the configured password is not leaked either, matching what api_response.go:222 already does for the API token.

triage.reason: There is no rate limiter or lockout in front of this comparison; server/middleware.go is the entire authentication layer for the web UI.
Remote timing measurement of a Go string comparison over HTTP is not a practical attack at this scale; per FP-10 the finding is downgraded to informational and kept, not deleted.

findings.limits: No timing measurement was taken. The claim is about a deviation from the codebase's own convention, not a demonstrated oracle.

findings.title: The external team-allowlist command is composed as a shell string from VCS-supplied repository and team names
findings.evidence: buildCommandString (external_team_allowlist_checker.go:48-60) builds one string by strings.Join of the operator's command, its extra args, the command name, ctx.BaseRepo.FullName and the team names formatted as `owner/team`, separated by spaces. That string is executed as `sh -c` at lines 27 and 37, and DefaultExternalTeamAllowlistRunner (server/core/runtime/external_team_allowlist_runner.go:24-25) passes it to exec.CommandContext as the shell's -c argument. BaseRepo.FullName and Owner come from the webhook payload via the event parser; team names come from VCSClient.GetTeamNamesForUser. Neither is quoted or escaped, and neither is validated for shell metacharacters or whitespace before this point - the codebase itself notes elsewhere that some providers permit spaces in repository owner names (server/core/runtime/apply_step_runner.go:73-75 and server/core/runtime/plan_step_runner.go:136-138 both call this out for Bitbucket Server).
findings.impact: At minimum, an identifier containing a space splits into extra positional arguments, so the operator's allowlist script sees a shifted argument vector and can decide wrongly - a fail-open in an authorization control. If any provider in scope permits a shell metacharacter in the values that reach line 59, the consequence is command execution as the Atlantis process.
findings.preconditions: The operator has configured an external team allowlist command (--gh-team-allowlist-command); the repository is in --repo-allowlist; and the attacker controls or can create a repository or team name carrying whitespace or a metacharacter on the configured provider.
findings.recommendation: Stop building a shell string. Pass the command and its arguments as an argv to exec.Command, as the codebase already does for terraform via models.NewArgvCommandRunner (server/core/runtime/models/shell_command_runner.go:80-93), so a metacharacter reaches the script as literal text. If a shell is genuinely required, quote every interpolated value.
findings.inference: That a repository full name or team name reaching line 59 can contain whitespace or a shell metacharacter on at least one supported provider. I did not enumerate the naming rules of GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps, and no validator in this tree constrains those fields before they arrive here.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The naming rules for repository path and team slug on each supported provider, or an integration test that drives ExternalTeamAllowlistChecker with a repo owner containing a space and asserts what the script receives in $1..$n.

triage.reason: No escaping or quoting exists on this path: buildCommandString joins with spaces at line 59 and the runner hands the result straight to `sh -c` (server/core/runtime/external_team_allowlist_runner.go:24-25).

Whether the interpolated values can carry a metacharacter depends on provider naming rules that are not stated anywhere in this tree; nothing in the repository constrains BaseRepo.FullName or the team names before line 59.
The checker is compiled in and selected at server/server.go when an external team allowlist command is configured; it is not test scaffolding.
There is no benign reading: `sh -c <joined string>` is shell source by construction, and the operator's own command is only the first token of it.

findings.limits: Establishes the unescaped composition and the shell sink. Does not establish that any supported provider actually permits a metacharacter in these fields, which is the one inferred link.

findings.title: The GitLab webhook validator writes the caller-supplied X-Gitlab-Token value into the error message it logs and returns
findings.evidence: On a token mismatch the validator returns `fmt.Errorf("header %s=%s did not match expected secret", secretHeader, headerSecret)` (line 57), interpolating the value the caller sent. handleGitlabPost (events_controller.go:629-631) passes err.Error() to e.respond, which logs it at Warn (events_controller.go:900-905) and writes it into the HTTP response body. The GitHub, Gitea and Bitbucket paths do not do this - they surface only the library's generic validation error.
findings.impact: None to the caller, who supplied the value. The effect is on the operator's logs: an anonymous client controls a string that lands verbatim in the server log at Warn level, which is a log-injection and log-noise surface, and the log is a place where a genuine secret pasted into the header by a misconfigured integration would then be stored in clear text.
findings.preconditions: --gitlab-webhook-secret configured and a request carrying a wrong X-Gitlab-Token.
findings.recommendation: Drop the value from the message: report only that the token did not match, matching the shape used by the other providers, and never echo a submitted credential into a log line or a response body.

triage.reason: The echoed value is the caller's own submitted header, not the configured secret, and it is returned only to the caller who sent it - so as a disclosure it grants the attacker nothing. It is kept as a logging-hygiene note, not a disclosure finding.
No redaction layer sits between the error and the log: events_controller.go:900-905 formats and logs the string as given.

findings.limits: No claim that a real secret is disclosed. The finding is that attacker-controlled text reaches the server log verbatim from an unauthenticated endpoint.

ruled_out.class: Missing or forgeable webhook signature verification
ruled_out.where: Read all five validators. GitHub delegates to github.ValidatePayload (github_request_validator.go:44); Bitbucket and Gitea use HMAC with hmac.Equal (vcs/common/request_validation.go:42, vcs/gitea/client.go:549); GitLab uses subtle.ConstantTimeCompare (gitlab_request_parser_validator.go:56); Azure DevOps uses basic auth (azuredevops_request_validator.go:44). All fail closed when the secret is configured. Bound: verification is skipped entirely when the corresponding secret is empty, which is the documented opt-out, not a defect in the check.

ruled_out.class: Repo-level atlantis.yaml escaping the server-side configuration boundary (custom workflows, apply requirements)
ruled_out.where: GlobalCfg.ValidateRepoCfg (server/core/config/valid/global_cfg.go:497-618) rejects every override key not present in allowed_overrides, rejects rCfg.Workflows unless allow_custom_workflows is true, and enforces allowed_workflows. Called on every parse from ParserValidator.parseRawRepoCfg (server/core/config/parser_validator.go:127). Bound: I did not test the merge itself (MergeProjectCfg, line 313) or autodiscover.

ruled_out.class: Path traversal via workspace, project name or drift API path selectors
ruled_out.where: valid.ValidateWorkspaceName (server/core/config/valid/workspace.go:36) rejects '/', '\\', '..', '.', leading '-' and '~', '$' and whitespace/control characters, and is applied both to comment workspaces (comment_parser.go:334) and to API path workspaces (api_controller.go:1037). models.NormalizeAPIPath and models.IsValidAPIWorkspace (server/events/models/drift.go:174-201) reject absolute, escaping and glob paths. Plan file paths are re-checked for containment by containedPlanRelPath (server/events/apply_plan_validator.go:299-310) and opened with os.OpenInRoot. Bound: the plan store under server/core/planstore was not read.

ruled_out.class: Argument injection into git through attacker-chosen refs and branch names
ruled_out.where: All git invocations use exec.Command with an argv (server/events/working_dir.go:834 wrappedGit, api_controller.go:612/681/688/695) and the fetch calls place `--` before the ref. models.IsUnsafeAPIRef (server/events/models/drift.go:106-124) rejects refs starting with '-' or '+', containing ':', or naming provider pull-request namespaces, and checkoutNonPRRef re-checks it at working_dir.go:765. Bound: no test was run; this is a code reading of the argv construction only.

ruled_out.class: GitHub Actions supply-chain exposure (unpinned actions, pull_request_target with code checkout, broad token permissions)
ruled_out.where: All 44 distinct `uses:` values across .github/workflows are pinned to a 40-character commit SHA. The two pull_request_target workflows (labeler.yml, pr-lint.yml) check out no code and declare least-privilege permissions blocks. Bound: organisation-level rulesets and branch protection live outside the repository and were not requested.

Repository-wide grep for the high-precision credential prefixes used by AWS access keys, GitHub personal-access tokens, Anthropic API keys, Slack bot tokens and PEM private-key headers returned only test fixtures (testdata/key.pem, testdata/key2.pem, server/events/vcs/github/testdata/fixtures.go) and documentation placeholders. Bound: no git history exists in this copy, so history was not scanned; no entropy-based scan was run.

server/controllers/web_templates/web_templates.go imports html/template, and the three plain-text responders (events_controller.go:903, locks_controller.go:153, jobs_controller.go:95) set Content-Type: text/plain. The template bodies under web_templates/templates/ were not read, so unescaped constructs inside them are unmeasured.

ruled_out.class: Dependency vulnerabilities in Go and npm dependencies
ruled_out.where: The engagement forbids consulting an advisory database, an upstream repository or a web search, so no SCA run and no reachability triage was possible; go.sum and package-lock.json were not analysed. What would unblock it: permission to run `govulncheck` / `npm audit` offline against a local advisory database. Nothing about the dependency set is claimed either way.
